name: Arm Triangle from Hindulotine
description: Master the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine in BJJ. Learn how guillotine defense creates head-and-arm choke opportunities with detailed finishing mechanics.
target_area: Carotid arteries (compressed by opponent's own shoulder and your arm)
summary: The Arm Triangle from Hindulotine is a head-and-arm blood choke that converts the opponent's own guillotine-defense frame into a trapped arm, compressing both carotids with their shoulder on one side and your forearm on the other.
overview:
The Arm Triangle from Hindulotine exploits the natural defensive reaction to guillotine pressure. When an opponent frames with their near arm to defend the Hindulotine grip, their own arm becomes trapped against their neck, creating the head-and-arm configuration needed for kata-gatame. The attacker transitions from guillotine mechanics to arm triangle compression, using the opponent's own shoulder as one blade of the choke while their forearm provides the opposing pressure on the other carotid artery.

This technique represents an advanced chain within the Hindulotine system that specifically punishes one of the most common defensive responses. Rather than forcing the guillotine against a strong frame, the practitioner recognizes when the opponent's arm position creates the arm triangle opportunity and flows into it seamlessly. The transition demands precise timing and constant head control to prevent the opponent from recovering posture or extracting their trapped arm during the grip switch.

The strategic value lies in the dilemma this creates within the Hindulotine attack system. Opponents who frame to defend the guillotine inadvertently set up the arm triangle. Those who keep their arms tight to prevent the arm triangle remain vulnerable to the original guillotine. This binary choice where both defensive responses feed the attacker's chain exemplifies modern submission grappling's emphasis on interconnected threat systems that force defensive errors.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential stroke risk if held too long

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from improper pressure angle
Shoulder compression injury to trapped arm

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum from lock to tap. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds.
tap_signals: Physical hand tap (multiple taps on opponent or mat)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with foot)
Any distress signal or loss of resistance
Immediately release if opponent goes limp
release_protocol: Immediately release arm squeeze and remove head pressure
Step back from opponent's head and shoulders
Allow opponent to breathe and recover (30-60 seconds)
Check for consciousness and normal breathing
If unconscious: position on side, elevate legs, monitor breathing until conscious
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - apply smooth progressive pressure only
Never hold after tap signal - release immediately upon any tap
Always allow tap access - do not trap both arms in training
Never use competition speed in training - practice control first
Stop immediately if opponent's face changes color (purple/red indicates excessive pressure)

variations_and_setups.description: The most common entry where the opponent frames against the Hindulotine grip with their near arm. You swim your choking arm over their frame and behind their neck, trapping their arm against their own carotid while transitioning to head-and-arm control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent creates a strong near-side frame to defend the guillotine pressure

variations_and_setups.description: After establishing the head-and-arm lock, you disengage your hips from the Hindulotine configuration and walk around to a perpendicular side control angle before applying the final squeeze. This provides maximum chest compression and eliminates space.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against larger or more flexible opponents who can create space when you finish from the initial Hindulotine angle

variations_and_setups.description: From bottom Hindulotine, you sweep the opponent using butterfly hooks while maintaining the head-and-arm grip throughout the transition. You finish the arm triangle from mount or transition to side control for the squeeze.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent drives forward into bottom Hindulotine and their weight loads onto your hooks

attacker.name: from Hindulotine Attacker
attacker.description: Step-by-step guide to finishing the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine. Learn grip transitions, finishing angles, and how to capitalize on guillotine defense.
attacker.overview: The Arm Triangle from Hindulotine attacks the carotid arteries using the opponent's own trapped shoulder combined with your forearm pressure. This finish capitalizes on one of the most common guillotine defenses: the near-side arm frame. When your opponent pushes their arm across to relieve guillotine pressure, they inadvertently position their arm against their own neck, creating the head-and-arm configuration. Your task is to recognize this moment, smoothly transition your grip from guillotine to arm triangle, and finish with progressive chest-to-chest compression while controlling the angle. The key advantage of entering from Hindulotine is that the rotational torque already breaks the opponent's posture and alignment, making the arm triangle finish more accessible than from a standard front headlock.
key_principles: Recognize the frame defense as the trigger to transition from guillotine to arm triangle rather than fighting the defense
Maintain constant head control throughout the grip switch to prevent posture recovery during the vulnerable transition moment
Drive the opponent's trapped arm tight against their own neck using chest pressure before attempting the squeeze
Walk your hips perpendicular to the opponent's body toward their trapped-arm side to create the optimal finishing angle
Use progressive chest-to-chest compression rather than arm squeezing to generate the choking pressure
Keep your head low and glued to the mat on the far side of opponent's head to seal the choke and prevent frame escapes
setup_requirements: Established Hindulotine position with guillotine grip secured on opponent's neck from top or bottom
Opponent has created a near-side arm frame across their own neck as a defensive response to the guillotine pressure
Your hips are positioned to allow disengagement from Hindulotine configuration and transition to side control angle
Sufficient control of opponent's posture to prevent them from standing up or extracting their head during the grip switch
Opponent's trapped arm is loaded against their own carotid with no space between their shoulder and neck

execution_steps.description: From your Hindulotine grip, feel the opponent push their near-side arm across their own neck to create a frame against your choking pressure. This arm crossing their neck is your trigger to transition. Do not fight the frame - instead, welcome it as the setup for the arm triangle.

execution_steps.action: Pin the trapped arm with chest pressure
execution_steps.description: Before releasing any part of your guillotine grip, drive your chest forward and down onto the opponent's framing arm, pinning it tight against their neck. Your body weight secures the arm in place while you prepare the grip transition. The arm must have no space between their shoulder and their neck.

Release your guillotine grip and immediately thread your choking arm over the opponent's trapped arm and behind the back of their neck. Your forearm crosses behind their neck with the blade pressing against the far-side carotid. Move smoothly without creating any gap that would allow head extraction.

execution_steps.action: Lock the figure-four or gable grip
execution_steps.description: Connect your hands by gripping your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind the opponent's head, or use a tight gable grip. The grip must lock the opponent's head and trapped arm together as a unit with no slack in the configuration.

Disengage your legs from the Hindulotine configuration and walk your hips around toward the opponent's trapped-arm side until you are perpendicular to their body. Your chest should be directly over their face. Each step tightens the choke by removing available space between your bodies.

execution_steps.action: Drop hip and seal the position
execution_steps.description: Drop your hip closest to their trapped arm to the mat, sprawling your weight onto the opponent. Your head drops low to the mat on the far side of their head. This seals the position and removes the space opponents use to breathe or create defensive frames. Your body acts as a wall.

Expand your chest while pulling your elbows together toward your own centerline. The opponent's trapped shoulder compresses one carotid artery while your forearm compresses the other. Apply slow, steady, progressive pressure rather than explosive squeezing. Wait for the tap or feel the resistance fade.

common_counters.counter: Opponent extracts trapped arm before grip is locked
common_counters.your_response: If the arm clears, immediately return to the Hindulotine guillotine grip since the opponent removed their own defense. Reset and wait for the frame to reappear.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and rolls toward the choking arm side
common_counters.your_response: Post your far-side hand and widen your base on the rolling side. If rolled, maintain the grip and finish from bottom using a guard arm triangle configuration.

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames with far arm to create space and prevent chest-to-chest pressure
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to strip their far-side frame by swimming inside their elbow. Walk further toward their head to collapse the space their frame creates.

common_counters.counter: Opponent pulls guard and locks closed guard to prevent hip walk-around
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the head-and-arm grip and work to open their guard by posting your knee into their tailbone. Once the guard opens, immediately walk to the finishing angle.

common_errors.error: Releasing guillotine grip too early before chest pressure secures the trapped arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent pulls their arm free during the transition, escaping both the guillotine and the arm triangle attempt, returning to a neutral position
common_errors.correction: Pin the opponent's framing arm with your chest weight before releasing any part of the guillotine grip. The arm must be immobilized by body pressure before you initiate the grip switch.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms instead of using chest compression and body angle
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly, the choke becomes ineffective, and the opponent can endure the pressure long enough to work an escape or wait for you to gas out
common_errors.correction: Walk to a perpendicular angle and use your dropping hip and expanding chest to generate pressure. Your arms lock the configuration in place while your body creates the compressive force.

common_errors.error: Leaving space between your chest and the opponent's trapped shoulder
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can breathe through the choke and create incremental space to extract their arm or work defensive frames
common_errors.correction: Drop your weight directly onto the opponent's face and trapped shoulder. Your chest must be flush against their body with zero gap. Think about melting your weight through them rather than hovering above.

common_errors.error: Failing to walk hips to perpendicular angle before squeezing
common_errors.consequence: The choke is applied at a suboptimal angle where the opponent's shoulder does not properly compress the carotid, resulting in a neck crank rather than a blood choke
common_errors.correction: Complete the full hip walk-around until you are at a 90-degree angle to the opponent's body. The chest-to-face alignment is what makes the opponent's own shoulder do the choking work.

common_errors.error: Keeping head high instead of dropping it to the mat on the far side
common_errors.consequence: Creates a gap on the far side that the opponent can use to turn their head and relieve pressure, or work their arm free through the space
common_errors.correction: Drop your head to the mat on the far side of the opponent's head immediately after walking to the finishing angle. Your head acts as a seal that prevents the opponent from turning away from the choke.

common_errors.error: Rushing the transition and losing the Hindulotine position entirely
common_errors.consequence: A sloppy transition gives the opponent time to recover posture, extract their head, and potentially counter to a dominant position
common_errors.correction: The transition should be smooth and deliberate, not explosive. Maintain constant pressure throughout. If the transition stalls, return to the Hindulotine guillotine grip rather than forcing a bad arm triangle.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the smooth switch from guillotine to head-and-arm configuration
training_progressions.description: Partner starts in Hindulotine bottom with their near arm across their neck in frame position. Practice the grip switch from guillotine to arm triangle with zero resistance, focusing on maintaining chest pressure on the trapped arm throughout the transition. Repeat 20 times per side. No finishing attempts.

training_progressions.focus: Walking to the correct angle and generating choke pressure through body mechanics
training_progressions.description: Start with the arm triangle grip already established. Partner gives 30% resistance. Practice walking your hips to the perpendicular angle, dropping your hip, and applying progressive chest compression. Partner provides feedback on pressure location and when the choke becomes effective. Alternate sides.

training_progressions.focus: Recognizing the frame defense and flowing from guillotine to arm triangle in live motion
training_progressions.description: Partner starts in Hindulotine bottom and alternates between defending with frames (triggering arm triangle) and defending without frames (staying in guillotine). Practice recognizing which defense is being used and flowing to the appropriate attack. 50% resistance, 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the full technique chain against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from Hindulotine top position. Partner gives 70-100% resistance with all defensive options available. Practice the full sequence: recognize frame, transition grip, walk to angle, finish. If the arm triangle fails, return to guillotine and try again. 5-minute rounds with full reset on escape.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine attack?
flashcards.answer: The arm triangle compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously. The opponent's own trapped shoulder presses into one carotid from the near side, while your forearm blade crosses behind their neck and presses into the opposite carotid from the far side. This bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds if not released.

trap: Crank the neck to force the tap

flashcards.question: How do you recognize when the opponent's defense creates the arm triangle opportunity from Hindulotine?
flashcards.answer: The trigger is the opponent creating a near-side arm frame across their own neck to relieve guillotine pressure. You will feel their forearm or hand pushing against your choking arm or their own neck. This frame positions their arm exactly where it needs to be for the arm triangle. The moment you feel this defensive frame, begin the transition rather than fighting to maintain the guillotine.

plausible: They post a hand on the mat

flashcards.question: What grip adjustment is required when transitioning from Hindulotine grip to arm triangle configuration?
flashcards.answer: Release the guillotine grip only after chest pressure secures the trapped arm against the opponent's neck. Thread your choking arm over the top of their trapped arm and behind the back of their neck so your forearm blade crosses the far-side carotid. Lock a figure-four grip by grabbing your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind their head, or use a gable grip for a tighter configuration.

trap: Let the arm slip, get passed

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to frame against your Hindulotine grip with their near arm - what adjustment capitalizes on this reaction?
flashcards.answer: Drive your chest down onto their framing arm to pin it against their own neck. Once the arm is secured by your body weight, smoothly transition your choking arm over the trapped arm and behind their neck to establish the head-and-arm lock. Do not try to strip the frame - instead, use it as the foundation for the arm triangle. Their defensive action becomes the setup for your next submission.

trap: Roll to your back to finish it

flashcards.question: What body angle creates maximum finishing pressure once the arm triangle is locked from Hindulotine?
flashcards.answer: Walk your hips until they are perpendicular (90 degrees) to the opponent's body on the trapped-arm side. Drop your near hip to the mat and place your head on the mat on the far side of their head. Your chest should be directly over their face. This angle allows your expanding chest and body weight to drive the opponent's shoulder into their own carotid while your forearm compresses the other side.

trap: Lean back; they bridge and reverse

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the arm triangle is properly locked and the opponent is approaching the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The choke is properly locked when you can feel the opponent's trapped shoulder bone pressing firmly into their neck with no space between your chest and their body. Their face will begin changing color as blood flow restricts. Their defensive movements become weaker and less coordinated. If they cannot create any frame with their free hand and cannot bridge effectively, they have passed the point of no escape.
flashcards.answer_line: No gap, face color, weak defense

trap: Hold the squeeze past the tap

flashcards.question: You have the head-and-arm locked but the choke stalls and the opponent is breathing comfortably - what is the most likely finishing error?
flashcards.answer: You are almost certainly squeezing with your arms instead of your body, and you have left space between your chest and their trapped shoulder. Stop pulling with the arms, finish walking your hips to a full perpendicular angle, drop your near hip to the mat, and melt your chest flush onto their trapped shoulder so their own deltoid drives into the carotid. The arms only lock the frame - the dropping hip and expanding chest create the kill.
flashcards.answer_line: Drop hip, flush chest, not arms

plausible: Pull their head with free hand
trap: Sit up to regrip, get reversed

flashcards.question: What competition finishing strategy maximizes the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine against a hard-defending opponent when the clock matters?
flashcards.answer: Use the dilemma rather than forcing one path: keep the guillotine threat live so any frame they give feeds the arm triangle, then commit to the grip the instant the frame appears. Once locked, immediately walk toward the trapped-arm side and finish from a near-side mount or kesa angle rather than staying square, because that angle pre-empts the bridge-and-roll escape and denies the referee a stalemate to stand up. Bait the frame, switch decisively, and finish off the angle before they can re-guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Bait the frame, walk trapped side

plausible: Stay square and grind it out
trap: Spin far side, they take your back

flashcards.question: What safety precautions must you observe when transitioning from Hindulotine guillotine to arm triangle pressure?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds, never spike or jerk the submission. Monitor the opponent's consciousness by feeling for resistance changes and watching for facial color changes. Always allow at least one hand free for tapping. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, hand, or foot taps. If the opponent goes limp, release immediately and place them in recovery position on their side.

plausible: Only stop for a verbal tap
trap: Squeeze harder if they go limp

flashcards.question: How do you prevent the opponent from extracting their trapped arm during the transition from Hindulotine to arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: The critical control is chest pressure on the trapped arm before and during the grip switch. Your body weight pins their arm against their own neck so they cannot pull it free. Once the head-and-arm grip is locked, the figure-four configuration mechanically prevents arm extraction. If you feel the arm starting to slide out during transition, immediately return to the Hindulotine guillotine grip rather than chasing a compromised arm triangle.

trap: Chase the arm out, get passed

defender.name: from Hindulotine Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine. Recognize the transition from guillotine, prevent the head-and-arm lock, and escape to safe positions.
defender.overview: Defending the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine requires recognizing the critical transition moment when the attacker shifts from guillotine to head-and-arm control. The primary danger window occurs when you frame against the guillotine, as this frame can be trapped and used against you. Successful defense demands awareness of arm positioning, immediate reactions to prevent the grip switch, and knowledge of escape timing. Early defense during the transition is far more effective than trying to escape a fully locked arm triangle, so understanding the attacker's sequence is essential for mounting an effective defense. The key defensive insight is that the arm triangle from Hindulotine requires a specific arm position from you, and controlling where your arm goes is your primary defensive tool.
key_principles: Defend the arm position first - keep your near arm either fully retracted against your body or fully extended away, never crossing your own neck
Recognize the transition moment when the attacker releases the guillotine grip as the highest-percentage escape window
Create distance by turning into the attacker rather than away to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
Frame against the attacker's hips and shoulders to prevent them from walking to the finishing angle
If caught, fight the angle by turning toward the attacker to relieve shoulder-on-carotid pressure
Tap early and clearly when the choke is locked - arm triangles restrict blood flow rapidly with minimal warning before unconsciousness
recognition_cues: The attacker drives their chest forward and down onto your framing arm, pinning it against your own neck with unusual deliberateness
The attacker releases their guillotine grip and begins threading their arm over your near arm and behind your neck
You feel the attacker's hips disengage from the Hindulotine leg configuration and begin walking toward your side
The attacker's head drops low to the mat on the far side of your head as they settle into the finishing position

defensive_options.action: Retract the framing arm before the grip switch completes
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the transition window when the attacker releases the guillotine grip to swim over your arm
defensive_options.if_successful: Arm escapes the trap, attacker must return to Hindulotine guillotine or front headlock without the arm triangle
defensive_options.risk: If timing is late, you may pull your arm deeper into the trap rather than free it

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and get to knees to prevent the finishing angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker begins walking their hips to the perpendicular angle but has not yet dropped their hip to seal
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing angle and can lead to a scramble back to Hindulotine control or turtle position
defensive_options.risk: Turning incorrectly can expose your back for a back take transition

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward the trapped arm side and pull guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the arm triangle is partially locked but the attacker has not fully sealed the position with their hip and head
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough space to pull the attacker into your closed guard where the arm triangle angle is disrupted
defensive_options.risk: A strong bridge against a well-positioned attacker may fail and waste energy

defensive_options.action: Walk feet toward attacker's hips and re-guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has locked the grip but is still adjusting their hip position
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing mechanics by pulling the attacker back into a guard position where they cannot generate chest compression
defensive_options.risk: If the choke is already tight, movement may accelerate the submission

escape_paths: Retract the near arm during the grip transition window and return to defending the Hindulotine guillotine
Turn into the attacker and get to knees to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
Bridge and shrimp toward the trapped arm side to create space and recover guard
Lock hands together and straighten the trapped arm to prevent the shoulder from compressing the carotid

favorable_outcomes.how: Retract your framing arm during the grip transition, preventing the arm triangle lock. The attacker returns to Hindulotine top position without the arm triangle, and you resume defending the guillotine.

Bridge powerfully toward the trapped arm side while pulling the attacker into your closed guard. The guard position disrupts the finishing angle and removes the chest compression needed to complete the choke.

common_errors.error: Framing across your own neck against the Hindulotine without awareness that this creates the arm triangle setup
common_errors.consequence: Your defensive frame becomes the trapped arm needed for the arm triangle, handing the attacker the submission on a plate
common_errors.correction: When defending the Hindulotine, keep your near arm either pinned tight to your own body or extended fully away from your neck. Never let your forearm cross your own throat line.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the attacker when caught in the arm triangle
common_errors.consequence: Turning away gives the attacker the perpendicular angle they need and drives your own shoulder deeper into your carotid, accelerating the choke
common_errors.correction: Always turn into the attacker toward the trapped arm side. This flattens the choke angle and prevents your shoulder from compressing your own carotid.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to defend and trying to escape after the arm triangle is fully locked and sealed
common_errors.consequence: A fully locked arm triangle with the hip dropped and head sealed is extremely difficult to escape. You waste energy fighting a near-certain submission and risk going unconscious.
common_errors.correction: Defend during the transition window when the attacker switches grips. This is when the attacker is most vulnerable. If the arm triangle is fully locked, tap early rather than risking unconsciousness.

common_errors.error: Pushing against the attacker's head instead of their hips when trying to create space
common_errors.consequence: Pushing the head does not disrupt the arm triangle mechanics and wastes arm energy that could be used for more effective escape movements
common_errors.correction: Frame against the attacker's hips and near shoulder to prevent them from walking to the angle. Hip frames disrupt the body mechanics that generate the choke, while head pushes do not.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from Hindulotine to an arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cue is feeling the attacker's chest weight drive down onto your framing arm, pinning it against your own neck, followed by the release of their guillotine grip as they begin threading their arm over yours and behind your neck. You may also feel their hips disengage from the Hindulotine leg configuration as they prepare to walk to the finishing angle.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in the Arm Triangle from Hindulotine?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately and clearly using any available signal: tap the mat or the attacker's body multiple times with your free hand, tap with your feet if hands are trapped, or verbally say 'tap' loudly. Do not wait to see if you can escape once the choke is locked - arm triangles compress the carotid arteries and can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds. Tapping early prevents injury and allows you to continue training.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap now: hand, foot, or voice

plausible: Slap the mat only, never them
trap: Ride it out and hope they slip

flashcards.question: What arm positioning prevents the attacker from converting the Hindulotine into an arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: Keep your near arm either pinned tight against your own body with your elbow down and hand on your own chest, or extend it fully away from your neck. The critical mistake is allowing your forearm to cross your own throat line, which creates the trapped-arm position the attacker needs. When defending the guillotine, use head positioning and hip movement rather than arm frames across your neck.
flashcards.answer_line: Elbow down, hand on your chest

plausible: Grab their belt with that arm
Push their head with both hands
trap: Cross your forearm at your throat

flashcards.question: The attacker has locked the head-and-arm configuration but has not yet walked to the finishing angle - what escape options remain?
flashcards.answer: This is your last high-percentage escape window. Turn into the attacker toward your trapped-arm side and fight to get to your knees. Simultaneously frame against their hips with your free arm to prevent them from walking to the perpendicular angle. If you can get your knees under you and face into the attacker, they cannot generate the chest compression needed to finish. Alternatively, bridge toward the trapped-arm side and pull them into closed guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn in, knees, frame their hips

plausible: Push their head with both hands
trap: Turn away and flatten your back

flashcards.question: What are the most common defensive errors that allow the arm triangle transition from Hindulotine?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is instinctively framing across your own neck when defending the guillotine, which directly creates the arm triangle setup. The second most common error is turning away from the attacker once caught, which accelerates the choke by driving your own shoulder into your carotid. The third is waiting too long to defend - the transition window when the attacker switches grips is the best escape opportunity, and it closes within 2-3 seconds.

trap: Turn away once the choke lands

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the transition cues from Hindulotine to arm triangle
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the Hindulotine to arm triangle transition at 25% speed. Practice recognizing each step: chest pressure on frame, grip release, arm swim, grip lock, hip walk. Call out each step as you feel it. No resistance, focus purely on building pattern recognition. 10 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Retracting the arm during the transition window
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the grip switch at 50% speed. Practice retracting your arm the moment you feel the guillotine grip release. Alternate between successful retractions and intentional failures where partner locks the arm triangle to build escape pattern recognition. 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Turning into the attacker and disrupting the finishing angle when caught
training_progressions.description: Start with the arm triangle already locked but not finished. Partner walks to the angle at 50-70% resistance. Practice turning into the attacker, framing against their hips, and working to recover guard or get to knees. Build the timing for when to bridge versus when to turn in. 3-minute rounds.

Partner starts in Hindulotine top with full offensive options. Defend all attacks including the arm triangle transition. Focus on arm positioning awareness to prevent the arm triangle setup while still defending the guillotine. 5-minute rounds, reset on escape or submission.

clips.title: The fastest escape out of the arm triangle
